middle-of-the-linked-list.pattern: Fast and slow pointers (fast moves two steps for each step of slow)

approaches.name: Copy the nodes into an array
approaches.idea: Put every node in an array; the middle (the second one for an even length) is at index `n / 2`.
steps: Walk the list and append each node to an array.
Return the node at index `n / 2` (integer division).
approaches.why: One pass to copy; the array holds all n node references.

approaches.name: Count, then walk half way
approaches.idea: Count the nodes in a first pass, then walk `n / 2` steps from the head in a second pass.
steps: Count the nodes: `n`.
Start at `head` and move `n / 2` times.
Return that node.
approaches.why: Two passes (n + n/2 steps) with only a counter and a pointer.

approaches.name: Slow and fast pointers in one pass
approaches.idea: Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps at a time. When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has covered half the distance and sits at the middle.
steps: Set `slow = fast = head`.
While `fast` and `fast.next` are not null: `slow = slow.next`, `fast = fast.next.next`.
Return `slow` (for an even length this is the second middle).
approaches.why: `fast` crosses the list once, so about n/2 iterations; two pointers of state.

approaches.name: Remember every node visited
approaches.idea: Walk the list storing each node in a hash set. Reaching a node that is already in the set means the list loops.
steps: Create an empty set of nodes.
Walk from `head`: if the current node is in the set, return true; otherwise add it and move on.
If the walk reaches null, return false.
approaches.why: Each node is visited once before a repeat is found or the end is reached; the set can hold all n nodes. Nodes are compared by identity, not value.

approaches.name: Floyd's slow and fast pointers
approaches.idea: Run two pointers, one step and two steps at a time. Without a cycle the fast one falls off the end; with a cycle both end up circling it and the fast one closes the gap by one node per step, so they must meet.
steps: Set `slow = fast = head`.
While `fast` and `fast.next` are not null: move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps.
If they point to the same node, return true.
If the loop ends, return false.
approaches.why: Once both are in the cycle, the gap shrinks by 1 each step, so they meet within one lap; before that, slow takes at most n steps. Only two pointers are stored.

happy-number.pattern: Cycle detection on an implicit sequence (n → sum of squares of digits)

approaches.name: Remember every value seen
approaches.idea: Keep applying the digit-square step. The sequence either reaches 1 or repeats a value (then it loops forever). A hash set spots the repeat.
steps: Create an empty set.
While `n != 1`: if `n` is in the set, return false; otherwise add it and replace `n` with the sum of the squares of its digits.
Return true when `n` becomes 1.
approaches.why: One step costs O(number of digits) = O(log n), and after the first step every value is below 1000 (a 10-digit number gives at most 10 × 81 = 810), so only a bounded number of steps follow. The set stores those few values.

approaches.name: Floyd's slow and fast pointers on the sequence
approaches.idea: Treat the numbers as a linked list where each value points to its digit-square sum. Run a slow pointer (one step) and a fast pointer (two steps); they meet inside the cycle, and the number is happy exactly when that cycle is the fixed point 1.
steps: Set `slow = n`, `fast = next(n)`.
While `fast != 1` and `slow != fast`: `slow = next(slow)`, `fast = next(next(fast))`.
Return `fast == 1`.
approaches.why: Same number of steps as before, up to a constant factor, but no set is stored.

palindrome-linked-list.pattern: Fast and slow pointers to find the middle, then reverse the second half

approaches.name: Copy the values into an array
approaches.idea: A singly linked list cannot be read backwards, but an array can. Copy the values and check them with two pointers.
steps: Walk the list and append each value to an array.
Compare `a[i]` with `a[n − 1 − i]` moving inwards; return false on a mismatch.
Return true.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the array holds all n values.

approaches.name: Reverse the second half in place and compare
approaches.idea: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half, and walk both halves together comparing values. Reverse the second half back afterwards so the input is left unchanged.
steps: Move `slow` one step and `fast` two steps until `fast` cannot move; `slow` is the start of the second half (the middle node of an odd list belongs to it, which is harmless).
Reverse the list starting at `slow`; call its new head `tail`.
Walk `p` from `head` and `q` from `tail` while `q` is not null, comparing values; remember any mismatch.
Reverse the second half again to restore the list, then return the result.
approaches.why: Finding the middle, two reversals and the comparison are each O(n). Only a few pointers are used.

remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.pattern: Two pointers with a fixed gap (lead pointer n steps ahead) + dummy head

approaches.name: Count the length, then remove in a second pass
approaches.idea: The n-th node from the end is node `L − n` from the start (0-based), where `L` is the length. Count `L`, then walk to the node just before it and unlink.
steps: Count the nodes: `L`.
Put a dummy node in front of `head` and walk `L − n` steps from the dummy; you are now just before the node to remove.
Skip it: `prev.next = prev.next.next`.
Return `dummy.next` (this handles removing the head).
approaches.why: Two passes over the list with a counter and a pointer.

approaches.name: One pass with a lead pointer n steps ahead
approaches.idea: Start two pointers at a dummy node and move the lead pointer `n` steps ahead. Then move both together; when the lead reaches the last node, the trailing pointer is just before the node to remove.
steps: Create `dummy` pointing to `head`; set `lead = trail = dummy`.
Move `lead` forward `n` times.
While `lead.next` is not null, move both `lead` and `trail` one step.
Unlink `trail.next` and return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: The lead pointer crosses the list once. The gap of exactly n nodes means `trail` stops n + 1 nodes before the end, right before the target.

linked-list-cycle-ii.pattern: Floyd's cycle detection, then a second walk to find the cycle's start

approaches.name: The first node visited twice
approaches.idea: Walk the list storing nodes in a hash set. The first node found already in the set is where the cycle begins.
steps: Create an empty set.
Walk from `head`; if the current node is in the set, return it; otherwise add it.
If the walk reaches null, return null.
approaches.why: Every node is visited once before the first repeat; the set can hold all n nodes.

approaches.name: Floyd's meeting point, then restart one pointer from the head
approaches.idea: Let `a` be the distance from the head to the cycle start and `c` the cycle length. When slow and fast meet, slow has walked some `d` steps and fast `2d`, so `d` is a multiple of `c`. Walking `a` more steps from the meeting point therefore lands on the cycle start — exactly where a pointer from the head arrives after `a` steps.
steps: Run slow (one step) and fast (two steps) from `head` until they meet; if fast reaches null, return null.
Move one pointer back to `head`, leave the other at the meeting point.
Move both one step at a time until they are the same node.
Return that node: the start of the cycle.
approaches.why: Both phases take at most about n steps. Only two pointers are used and the list is not modified.

reorder-list.pattern: Find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half, merge the halves alternately

approaches.name: Array of nodes and two pointers
approaches.idea: Store the nodes in an array, then relink them by taking from the front and the back alternately.
steps: Copy every node into an array `a`.
With `i = 0`, `j = n − 1`: while `i < j`, set `a[i].next = a[j]`, move `i` right; if `i == j` stop; set `a[j].next = a[i]`, move `j` left.
Set `a[i].next = null` to end the list.
approaches.why: One pass to copy and one to relink; the array holds n node references.

approaches.name: Middle, reverse, merge — all in place
approaches.idea: The new order interleaves the first half with the second half read backwards. So split at the middle, reverse the second half, and weave the two lists together.
steps: Find the end of the first half with slow/fast pointers (`fast` starts at `head`, loop while `fast.next` and `fast.next.next` exist), so the first half is never shorter.
Cut the list after `slow`, and reverse the part that followed it.
Merge: take one node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, until the second half runs out.
approaches.why: Each of the three phases is one linear pass; only a few pointers are used.

find-the-duplicate-number.pattern: Floyd's cycle detection on index → value links (array as a linked list)

approaches.name: Compare every pair
approaches.idea: The repeated value is the one that two different positions share.
steps: For each `i` and each `j > i`, compare `nums[i]` and `nums[j]`.
The first equal pair gives the duplicate: return `nums[i]`.
approaches.why: About n²/2 comparisons. It respects the rules (no changes, O(1) space) but is too slow for n = 10⁵.

approaches.name: Hash set (or a seen array)
approaches.idea: Remember every value seen; the first value seen twice is the duplicate.
steps: Keep a boolean array `seen` of size n + 1 (values are 1..n).
For each value: if `seen[x]`, return `x`; otherwise mark it.
approaches.why: One pass, but the extra array breaks the O(1) space rule.

approaches.name: Binary search on the value (pigeonhole counting)
approaches.idea: For a guess `mid`, count how many values are `<= mid`. Without a duplicate at or below `mid` that count is at most `mid`; if it is larger, the duplicate is in `1..mid`. This halves the value range each time.
steps: Set `lo = 1`, `hi = n` (n = `nums.length − 1`).
While `lo < hi`: `mid = (lo + hi) / 2`; count values `<= mid`.
If the count is greater than `mid`, set `hi = mid`; otherwise `lo = mid + 1`.
Return `lo`.
approaches.why: log n rounds, each counting over the whole array. No extra memory and the array is not changed.

approaches.name: Floyd's cycle detection on i → nums[i]
approaches.idea: Read the array as a linked list where index `i` points to index `nums[i]`. Every value is in 1..n, so nothing points back to index 0: the walk from 0 must eventually enter a cycle. The duplicate value is pointed to by two different indices, so it is exactly where the path joins the cycle — the cycle's entrance.
steps: Start `slow` and `fast` at index 0; move `slow = nums[slow]` and `fast = nums[nums[fast]]` until they meet.
Reset `slow = 0`.
Move both one step at a time (`slow = nums[slow]`, `fast = nums[fast]`) until they are equal.
Return that value: the entrance of the cycle, i.e. the duplicate.
approaches.why: The same argument as Linked List Cycle II: both phases take O(n) steps, two integers of state, and the array is only read.
